blocks.label: The reset click
blocks.content:
Every 20 minutes after hour 2, you run a 10-second body scan. It becomes as automatic as looking at your power meter.

Heavy feet? Check. Quiet hands? ... No. Grip is at a 6. You consciously drop it to a 3. Elbows bent? They'd drifted straight — you bend them. Hinge moving? Hips had locked — you rock your pelvis once. Breathing anchored? You'd been shallow-chesting for who knows how long — you take three belly breaths. Eyes on far target? Your scan had contracted — you push your focal point back to 50 meters.

There's a moment — maybe a half-second — where the corrections land and the whole system re-engages. Your body settles into the pattern you drilled fresh. The front wheel starts floating over bumps again instead of smashing through them. Your line choice opens up. Your braking becomes proactive instead of reactive.

That's the click. It's the sensation of the right pattern re-engaging after fatigue has silently disengaged it. It doesn't last forever — fatigue will erode it again in 15-20 minutes. That's why you scan again. The click is not permanent. It's renewable.

blocks.title: A late-ride check
blocks.content:
Late in a long gravel ride, a rider approaches a bend they would usually read without trouble. Their hands are pressing hard on the bars and they notice the loose patch only at the turn. They slow abruptly and have to widen their line.

Fatigue can make it harder to notice a change in grip, posture, or attention. When the ride starts to feel more difficult to manage, give yourself more space, lower your pace, and check whether you can still see and choose a line. Stop to rest or seek help if you cannot ride with control.

Everything from Lessons 1-11 was built for this moment — when your body wants to quit being skilled and your brain has to intervene.

Technique doesn't just fade with fatigue. It degrades in a specific, predictable sequence that's invisible from the inside. You feel "tired." What's actually happening is systematic loss of motor patterns. The good news: predictable means catchable.

### The Fatigue Cascade

Skill degradation follows a consistent order. Fitness, nutrition, heat, and course difficulty shift the timeline — but the sequence is remarkably stable.

items.title: Fatigue Cascade Neuroscience: Stages and Mechanisms

L1: weighted drop inverts, forearm fatigue accelerates
Dead spots grow, mashing replaces smooth stroke, cadence drifts lower
L1: pedal weighting, L7: rear-wheel spin on loose surfaces
Scan contracts 50m to 15m, geometric lines replace surface-optimal
L4 + L6 + L8 + L9: cornering, surface reading, descending
Braking in corners, grabbing rear, panic-stopping
L1+L4+L5+L6+L8+L9 compound loss — surviving, not riding
blocks.caption: Fatigue Cascade Stages

blocks.content: The cascade follows the neurological hierarchy of motor control. Grip escalation (Stage 1) happens first because it's a reversion to the brainstem's startle-grip reflex — the oldest motor pattern, and the one the brain defaults to under stress and resource depletion. Stages 2-3 involve prefrontal and cerebellar coordination that degrades as blood glucose drops and core temperature rises. Stage 4 is the compound failure: when scan distance contracts AND grip escalates AND the hinge freezes, the rider has lost the feedforward planning loop entirely and is operating in pure reactive mode — stimulus → response, no anticipation. The body scan interrupts this cascade by forcing conscious re-engagement of the prefrontal planning loop, even briefly.

### Notice grip and control

On a safe stretch, ask whether your hands are tense, your sightline is clear, and your braking still feels smooth. Keep your fingers securely on the controls. If steering or braking feels less reliable, slow down, create space, and choose easier ground. Stop or walk if control does not return. A timed finger-lift test is not needed.

### The Full Body Scan — 10 Seconds

This is the reset protocol. Run it every 20 minutes after hour 2, or immediately when the pinky check fails.

1. **Feet** (2 seconds): Check that your pedals feel heavy — your feet supporting you without hanging on the bars. If your feet feel light and your hands feel heavy, push weight down. Drop your heels 10 degrees. This is Lesson 1.

2. **Hands** (2 seconds): Confirm grip at 3 out of 10, fingers wrapped loosely. If you're clamping, consciously release until the bars feel like a shelf your hands are resting on. This is Lesson 1.

3. **Elbows and shoulders** (2 seconds): Elbows should be bent 20 degrees, shoulders dropped away from ears. If your arms are straight and your shoulders are up, you've lost the suspension system from Lesson 2. Bend and drop.

4. **Hips** (2 seconds): Check that the hinge is moving. Rock your pelvis forward and back once. If your lower back feels locked and your vision is bouncing, the hinge has frozen. One conscious hip-rock resets it. This is Lesson 2.

5. **Eyes and breath** (2 seconds): Notice whether you're looking 50 meters ahead or just 15. Push the focal point out to 3-5 seconds ahead. Take one deep belly breath. Exhale completely. This is Lesson 4.

Ten seconds. Five checkpoints. Each one maps to a skill you've already drilled. The scan doesn't teach you anything new — it re-engages what fatigue has silently disengaged.

### Two-Rule Mode

At hour 5+, you can't hold 11 lessons in working memory. Cognitive load shedding: reduce everything to two rules for the current terrain.

- **Rolling gravel descent**: (1) Eyes 50 meters ahead. (2) Brakes before corners, not in them.
- **Loose gravel climb**: (1) Stay seated. (2) Spin, don't mash.
- **Technical singletrack**: (1) Light hands. (2) Look where you want to go.

Two rules you can actually hold are worth more than ten you can't. Rotate as terrain changes — you're choosing from a list you've already internalized.

Motor sequences survive better than decisions
blocks.caption: What You Built, What Fatigue Takes

blocks.content: Foundational skills (grip, hinge) degrade first — overridden by survival instincts. Complex skills (line choice, pacing) degrade because they require cognitive processing that fatigue erodes. The body scan catches the early ones. Two-rule mode protects the later ones.

blocks.title: Fatigue Awareness Ride
blocks.description: On a familiar, low-risk route, notice how your vision, grip, braking, and line choice change as you tire. Do not seek technical terrain or a fixed duration to prove fatigue tolerance. Turn home or stop when control fades.

variants.label: Easy route check
steps: Choose a familiar route with clear sightlines and an easy way home. Bring the food, water, and repair supplies you normally need.
Early in the ride, note whether your feet support you, your hands are secure, and you can see and choose a line comfortably.
Repeat the same brief check later. If your grip tightens, vision narrows, or braking becomes abrupt, slow down, choose easier ground, and consider ending the ride.
After stopping safely, write down the first cue that changed and what helped you recover control.

proof_gate.description: You can notice a change in control and respond by reducing difficulty.
proof_gate.target: Record one fatigue cue and the safe adjustment you made; no pace, duration, or score target

blocks.question: You're at hour 4 of a 6-hour gravel race. You run the pinky check and it feels dangerous — like lifting your pinkies might cost you control. You also notice you've been braking in corners for the last 20 minutes. What fatigue cascade stage are you in, and what's the correction sequence?

options.text: Stage 1 only — just grip pressure. Loosen your hands and keep riding.
Stage 4 — reactive braking. Focus on braking earlier before corners.
Stages 1 and 4 simultaneously — run the full body scan, reset grip first, then push scan distance out to restore proactive braking zones.
You're beyond correction — slow down and survive to the finish.

blocks.explanation: The failed pinky check confirms Stage 1 (grip pressure). Braking in corners confirms Stage 4 (reactive braking). But Stage 4 doesn't happen in isolation — if you're braking reactively, it's because your scan distance contracted (Stage 3) and your grip escalation (Stage 1) has been compounding for at least an hour. The correction starts at Stage 1 because grip is the foundation: run the full body scan, reset grip to a 3, bend your elbows, drop your shoulders. Then push your eyes back to 50 meters ahead — this restores the visual lead time you need to set speed BEFORE corners instead of braking IN them. You're not beyond correction. You're exactly where the scan was designed to catch you. The click is available. You just have to run the sequence.

### The Deliberate Practice Framework

The progression from here isn't more lessons — it's repetition under increasingly demanding conditions until the skills become how you ride.

Pick a 20-min block. Announce the skill. Rate execution 1-10.
Body scan every 20 min after hour 2. Rate skills proof segments. Track scores.
Don't wait for fatigue — start with 2 rules for opening terrain. Rotate as terrain changes.
L11 skills decay fastest. After a ride. Outdoors. Timed.
blocks.caption: Ongoing Practice Schedule

blocks.content: Your field notes are the artifact of this course. Keep the tire setup you tested, the gearing you have ridden on a comparable climb, and the handling cues that worked on familiar terrain. Put only the cues you can use at a glance on a stem note. The note should help you make conservative decisions when you are tired, not promise a corner speed or stopping distance.

### Take the practice into the next ride

These 21 lessons give you drills and cues. The value comes from repeating them on the bike, checking what happens, and changing one thing at a time.

Pick one cue for your next ride. Choose a low-risk place to practice it. Write down what changed and what still felt uncertain. The course ends here; the practice continues on your own roads.
On a familiar ride, notice one fatigue cue and how you adjusted. Reduce pace or end the ride if your line choice, vision, or braking becomes unreliable.

This course is training wheels you're meant to grow out of. The drills had structure so you could learn without structure. The proof gates had numbers so you could eventually ride without numbers. The body scan had a checklist so that one day, you won't need the checklist — your body will just click back into the right pattern on its own. That's the goal. Not lessons memorized. Skills practiced enough that you no longer have to name them. See you on the gravel.
